findings.title: WordPress core version 5.2 exposed and outdated
findings.explanation: The site is running WordPress 5.2, which is a very old version of the software. Old WordPress versions are missing years of security fixes, making the site an easy target for automated attacks that scan for known vulnerabilities.
findings.recommendation: Update WordPress core to the latest stable release as soon as possible, after taking a full backup.

findings.title: Outdated plugins and theme in use
findings.explanation: The site uses Contact Form 7 version 4.9 and Yoast SEO version 10.0, along with the Twenty Nineteen theme version 1.0. Old plugin and theme versions often have publicly known security holes that attackers can exploit to take over a site.
findings.recommendation: Update all plugins and the theme to their latest versions, or remove any that are no longer needed.

findings.title: Server running outdated PHP version 7.2.1
findings.explanation: The web server is exposing PHP 7.2.1 in its response headers. This PHP version is long past its supported life, meaning it no longer receives security updates, which increases the risk of the server being compromised.
findings.recommendation: Upgrade the server's PHP version to a currently supported release (check with your hosting provider).

findings.title: WordPress REST API exposes user account information
findings.explanation: The site's REST API is publicly revealing user account details (3 user accounts were found). Attackers commonly use this information to build a list of valid usernames to target with password-guessing attacks.
findings.recommendation: Restrict or disable the WordPress REST API user endpoint, or use a security plugin to block unauthenticated access to user data.

findings.title: XML-RPC endpoint is enabled
findings.explanation: The XML-RPC interface (xmlrpc.php) is active on the site. This feature is frequently abused by attackers to perform brute-force login attempts and to amplify denial-of-service attacks against the site.
findings.recommendation: Disable XML-RPC unless it is actively required by a plugin or integration, using a security plugin or server-level rule.

findings.title: WordPress readme.html file is publicly accessible
findings.explanation: The default readme.html file that ships with WordPress is accessible to anyone. This file can reveal the exact WordPress version installed, helping attackers identify which vulnerabilities might apply to the site.
findings.recommendation: Delete or block access to the readme.html file in the WordPress installation directory.

findings.title: TLS certificate expires in 60 days
findings.explanation: The site's SSL/TLS certificate is valid for 60 more days. While not urgent, if it is not renewed in time visitors will see security warnings and be blocked from accessing the site.
findings.recommendation: Set up automatic renewal for the Let's Encrypt certificate, or add a calendar reminder to renew before it expires.

findings.title: No DMARC email policy configured
findings.explanation: The domain has an SPF record but no DMARC record. Without DMARC, it's easier for attackers to send emails that impersonate this domain, which can be used for phishing against your customers or partners.
findings.recommendation: Add a DMARC DNS TXT record (e.g., starting with a monitoring policy) to help protect the domain from email spoofing.

findings.title: Server only offers TLS 1.2, not TLS 1.3
findings.explanation: The connection to the site negotiated using TLS 1.2. TLS 1.2 is still considered acceptable, but TLS 1.3 offers better security and performance and is now widely supported.
findings.recommendation: Enable TLS 1.3 support on the web server if the hosting environment allows it.
